ancient_source: Arabic conquest narratives compiled by al-Baladhuri (Futuh al-Buldan) and al-Tabari (Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk)
modern_citation: Kaegi, W.E., Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests, Cambridge University Press, 1992 (Byzantine force probably did not exceed 20,000); cf. Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium, Cambridge University Press, 2003, giving 15,000-20,000
notes: Early Arabic conquest narratives give Byzantine strength as 100,000-200,000+; later legendary accounts (pseudo-Waqidi's Futuh al-Sham tradition) inflate this further to 400,000-800,000. Kaegi argues 7th-century Byzantine logistics and the post-Persian-war manpower crisis could not sustain a field army much above 20,000. Note the modern range is itself contested: Treadgold argues for a much higher 80,000-100,000, so this log-ratio should be read as one defensible point in a genuine scholarly spread, not a settled consensus.

ancient_source: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk (transmitting Sayf ibn Umar's account)
modern_citation: Donner, F.M., The Early Islamic Conquests, Princeton University Press, 1981, Appendix G (available: https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt7zvcmx)
notes: This case runs opposite to the usual enemy-inflation pattern: it is the Muslim futuh chroniclers' account of their OWN side that looks inflated against Donner's conservative reconstruction of the muqatila (fighting-men) rolls, not the Sasanian enemy. The widely repeated Sasanian figure (50,000-100,000+ in most secondary literature) could not be traced to a specific named academic monograph independent of the same Sayf ibn Umar chronicle tradition that modern historians (Donner included) treat as unreliable for numbers, so no Sasanian-side case is included here -- that side is judged to have no settled modern consensus distinct from the ancient claim itself.

modern_citation: Amitai-Preiss, R., Mongols and Mamluks: The Mamluk-Ilkhanid War, 1260-1281, Cambridge University Press, 1995
notes: Hulegu withdrew most of the Ilkhanid army east for the 1260 kurultai after Mongke Khan's death, leaving Kitbuqa with a small holding force in Syria. The Mamluk chronicler al-Yunini nonetheless reports the nominal strength of the full Mongol field army (100,000) rather than the detachment actually present. Amitai-Preiss reconstructs 10,000-12,000 from Mongol tumen organisation. This looks like scope conflation (whole-army figure applied to a fraction of it) layered on top of ordinary chronicle inflation, a distinct failure mode from simple exaggeration.

modern_citation: Haldon, J., The Byzantine Wars: Battles and Campaigns of the Byzantine Era, Tempus, 2001, p. 180
notes: Matthew of Edessa was an Armenian chronicler, not a direct combatant on either side, so this is classified 'neutral' rather than 'enemy_of_author'; contemporaneous Muslim sources independently converge on similarly inflated Byzantine figures, so the inflation is not confined to one historiographic tradition. Haldon's 40,000 is given as a point estimate rather than a range in the cited work. Close to half the Byzantine force reportedly deserted or defected (Turkic mercenaries changed sides) before contact, a command-cohesion detail worth capturing separately from the raw headcount.

ancient_source: Johann Schiltberger, Reisebuch (eyewitness memoir of a captured Bavarian squire)
modern_citation: Nicolle, D., Nicopolis 1396: The Last Crusade, Osprey Campaign Series 64, Osprey Publishing, 1999
notes: Schiltberger's figure is the extreme end even among Crusader-side chroniclers; some later German 19th-century historians gave far lower estimates (12,000-20,000) on logistical grounds long before Nicolle. Nicolle's reconstruction puts both armies at rough parity (~15-16,000 each), implying Nicopolis was a tactical rather than a numerical defeat for the Crusaders. See the companion case nicopolis_crusader for the mirror-image inflation running the other way.

modern_citation: Nicolle, D., Nicopolis 1396: The Last Crusade, Osprey Campaign Series 64, Osprey Publishing, 1999
notes: Sukrullah, an Ottoman court historian writing in the 1460s, gives the mirror image of nicopolis_ottoman: the Christian force inflated rather than the Ottoman one. Read together, both belligerents' own chroniclers inflate the enemy by a similar order of magnitude (8x-13x) relative to Nicolle's modern reconstruction, which argues the exaggeration mechanism here is symmetric across the Christian/Ottoman divide rather than a quirk of one tradition.

ancient_source: Ibn Arabshah, Aja'ib al-Maqdur fi Nawa'ib Timur
modern_citation: Tucker, S.C. (ed.), Battles That Changed History: An Encyclopedia of World Conflict, ABC-CLIO, 2010, p. 140
notes: Ibn Arabshah was a Damascene scholar carried off by Timur as a youth who came to despise him; his hostile biography's 800,000 figure is flagged by modern historians as unrealistic, alongside an even higher 1.6 million reported by a German eyewitness elsewhere in the tradition. The Tucker figure is a reference-encyclopedia entry rather than a specialist Timurid monograph; a dedicated academic reassessment (e.g. at Beatrice Forbes Manz's level of detail) specifically for Ankara could not be located in the time available, so this case should be weighted with that caveat.

ancient_source: Nicolo Barbaro, Giornale dell'assedio di Costantinopoli (Venetian eyewitness siege diary)
modern_scholar: Marios Philippides and Walter K. Hanak
modern_citation: Philippides, M. and Hanak, W.K., The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453: Historiography, Topography, and Military Studies, Ashgate/Routledge, 2011
notes: Barbaro was present at the siege as a crossbowman, so this is an eyewitness diary rather than a later legendary chronicle, yet it still runs roughly double the modern consensus range. Other contemporary chroniclers (Greek sources writing soon after) go much higher, to 300,000-400,000; Barbaro's 160,000 is comparatively conservative among contemporary claims. Philippides and Hanak's monograph is the standard modern military-historiographical treatment and interrogates the primary figures source by source.

side_label: Constantinople's defenders (Byzantine subjects and foreign contingents)
ancient_source: George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (records the civic muster Constantine XI ordered before the siege)
modern_citation: Runciman, S., The Fall of Constantinople 1453, Cambridge University Press, 1965
notes: This is the case the project most needs: a genuinely administrative source, not a rhetorical one. Sphrantzes reports the result of an actual census the emperor ordered of every district's tribunes -- 4,773 Greek subjects able to bear arms plus 200 foreigners he could enumerate -- and modern historians treat this as essentially reliable for what it counts. Modern totals nearer 7,000 (following Runciman) add Genoese and Venetian mercenary companies operating under their own captains (e.g. Giovanni Giustiniani's contingent), documented in Italian sources outside Sphrantzes' civic census. The negative log-ratio here is not chronicle exaggeration but an administrative source undercounting a category (foreign mercenaries) that fell outside its own jurisdictional scope -- a different failure mode from inflation, and worth keeping distinguishable if the two get pooled into one prior.

ancient_source: Babur, Baburnama (Waqi'at-i Baburi) -- describes Ibrahim's standing army as 'a lak' (100,000)
modern_citation: Chandra, S., Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part I: Delhi Sultanat (1206-1526), Har-Anand Publications (exact edition/page not independently verified in this session)
notes: Babur is describing the enemy in his own memoir, so this is a first-person military autobiography rather than a later compiled chronicle, though classified 'chronicle' here for lack of a better bucket. Of all the enemy-inflation cases in this set the ratio is comparatively modest (round number 'a lak' vs. a modern range whose upper bound nearly reaches it), consistent with Babur's memoir being generally regarded as one of the more matter-of-fact primary sources of the period.

ancient_source: Mewari court-bardic tradition (Ranchhod Bhatt, Rajprashasti Mahakavya, c.1670s-1710; compiled in Kaviraj Shyamaldas, Vir Vinod, 19th c.)
modern_citation: Chandra, S., Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part II: Mughal Empire (1526-1748), Har-Anand Publications (exact edition/page not independently verified in this session)
notes: Unusually, the inflated figure here comes from the DEFEATED side's own bardic-epic tradition (Mewar), glorifying Maharana Pratap's stand by magnifying the Mughal force he faced, rather than the more typical case of a victor inflating a defeated enemy. Akbar's own court chronicle (Akbarnama) gives different and generally lower Mughal-side numbers, so the two traditions disagree in the opposite direction from Yarmouk/Ain Jalut/Nicopolis. Treat 'chronicle' loosely here -- Rajprashasti is verse epic (mahakavya), not prose annal, closer to the pseudo-Waqidi genre than to Barbaro's diary.

ancient_source: Winston S. Churchill, The River War: An Account of the Reconquest of the Soudan, 1899 ('an army of more than 60,000 men')
modern_citation: Spiers, E.M. (ed.), Sudan: The Reconquest Reappraised, Frank Cass, 1998
notes: Churchill was a serving cavalry officer at the battle, and his figure draws on British military intelligence reconnaissance rather than folk tradition or literary convention; it sits within, or just above, the modern scholarly range rather than far outside it, making this one of the more faithful cases in the set. Modern estimates for Mahdist strength are themselves fairly wide (35,000-60,000 across different accounts), which is itself informative: even a well-documented colonial-era battle with surviving order-of-battle paperwork on the British side has real uncertainty on the opposing side's numbers.
